Replace.Text: Gold gets a market. Borrow from other civilizations or a bond market, lend to a neighbour who's short, set your taxes with a policy card, and let an auto-loan guard keep you clear of the game's negative-balance penalties; a missed payment or a repudiated debt costs you your good name. Resources get world prices, trading partners settle what they owe each other every turn, and you can put a tariff on a partner or invest in a neighbour's builds and treasury. Wars, disasters and debt push the world through booms and slumps, inflation can eat into idle Gold, old markets and banks fade across the ages, and your government sets how your economy runs. The computer players play by the same rules. Single-player.
Whether civilizations can borrow from each other and, later, from a bond market, within a limit set by income. Off turns the loans off; trade bills and investment keep their own options.

When your treasury is about to fall below the line where the game starts taking amenities, the guard takes out an emergency loan for you, up to a cap of ten turns of your income. You can also switch it on the Loans tab.
You borrow only when you ask to. The game's penalties for a negative balance apply as usual.
An emergency loan covers a shortfall before the game's penalties start, until the cap is reached. You're told once when it is.
Whether the computer players take part: borrowing when they run short, lending when they're flush, restructuring an overdue loan, and now and then repudiating a debt to an enemy.

A quarter above the standard rates. Debt bites sooner and lending pays more.

Adds the tax policy cards: Light Taxation, Heavy Taxation and War Levy. Each trades Gold against happiness in one of your ordinary policy slots, and the computer players choose among them as they do any card.

Gives every resource a world price, set by how many copies there are and who needs them. Each pair of civilizations then settles the net value of what they import from each other every turn, and a civilization pays at most a tenth of its income this way.
Resources don't get a world price, and a route costs the importer what it does in the base game.
Bills open with the Trade stage (Code of Laws in Antiquity) and show on the Trade tab.

Lets a civilization hold back part of what it owes the civilizations it imports from: 10 percent at Low, 25 at High. A High tariff costs relationship with each partner it bills. Needs Markets and trade bills.

Tariffs open with Imperialism, on the Fiscal tab. The computer players set their own and answer yours in kind.
Lets civilizations put Gold into each other: a development loan on a city's current build, a general investment in its treasury, or either one as aid, which isn't paid back.
Each civilization keeps its Gold at home.

When the civilizations with Public debt owe the bond market a lot beside the Gold they hold, the Gold each of them keeps above a reserve of twenty turns of income slowly loses value, and bond loans get dearer. Off by default.
Bond debt erodes idle Gold above the reserve and raises bond rates.

Wars, captures, disasters, the age's crisis, defaults and changes in trade move a world economic index and each civilization's own economy through booms and slumps. A boom pays a little Gold each turn and makes bonds cheaper; a slump takes a little and makes them dearer.
Events move the economy half as much.
Events move the economy by their full weight.
Events move the economy half again as much.

Each civilization's government, or its ideology in the Modern age, sets how its economy runs: Despotism lives on tribute, a Classical Republic borrows from its citizens, Communism plans production, and more. The Fiscal tab shows what yours changes. Each computer player leans toward a government that suits its civilization, so they spread across the systems.
Every civilization runs a mixed economy.
Government and ideology set each civilization's economic system.
A bit of everything: standard rates and credit, and the world's booms and slumps reach you at their usual strength.
Private capital and price signals: bonds cost 10 percent less and your economy recovers from a slump faster, but a Panic hits you harder.
You take wealth to pay for expansion: Heavy Taxation and War Levy bring more Gold, your aid buys twice the goodwill, and you borrow only from other civilizations, at 20 percent more.

Your citizens fund the state: you can borrow from them, and the interest comes back as celebration. Light Taxation celebrates more and Heavy Taxation costs more Happiness. Your Trade buildings move bills by 12 percent each and your Commerce buildings count a quarter more.
Finance runs the state: you borrow and lend at 20 percent less, your credit limit is 4 turns of income higher, and booms and slumps swing you harder, a Panic most of all.

Local stability over money: taxes come in kind, half the Gold and half the Happiness cost. You pay 20 percent less on trade bills, your warehouses shelter twice as much from a slump, the world's swings reach you less, and your credit limit is 4 turns lower.

You get rich exporting: you're owed 10 percent more on bills, a High tariff costs relationship half as often, bonds cost 20 percent less, your investments earn a point more, and booms and slumps swing you harder.
Interest is forbidden: what you lend comes back as a share that follows the borrower's income, and your aid buys twice the goodwill.

Capital goes to industry and war: War Levy pays its full wartime amount in peace too, a war booms your own economy and peace brings it down, your credit limit is half again as large and bonds cost 25 percent less, idle Gold erodes twice as fast, your factories count twice for demand, and you take development loans only.

The treasury becomes production: a fifth of your Gold income goes into your cities' builds each turn, you buy at fixed prices, the world's booms and slumps pass you by, you borrow only from other civilizations and you take development loans only.
